name: Benzoyl peroxide wash for body odor

lead: Benzoyl peroxide wash is borrowed from acne care and used on the armpits and body for a fresher smell.

It is an oxidizer sold over the counter and on the WHO list of essential medicines. For acne it is thought to kill Cutibacterium acnes through oxidative damage, reduce sebum and unclog pores. Proponents extend this to odor bacteria; Wikipedia does not mention body odor use and no studies of it were found.

paras: Applied as a wash in the shower to underarms or body, left on briefly and rinsed, often in a routine alongside deodorant.
Irritation is common, about 1 in 500 people have hypersensitivity, and phototoxicity occurs. It can permanently bleach fabrics and towels.

angle.text: An acne wash repurposed for armpits and body, used on the idea that it kills odor-producing bacteria. Its antibacterial role in acne is well established; no studies have tested it for odor.

lead: Benzoyl peroxide is an oxidizer used mainly as an acne medication, sold over the counter and on the WHO list of essential medicines.[1] In looksmaxxing and body-care discussions, benzoyl peroxide washes are applied to the armpits or body to cut odor-producing bacteria, so that a person smells fresher and has cleaner-feeling skin, which feeds into overall presentation.

Underarm odor arises when skin bacteria such as Corynebacterium break down compounds in apocrine sweat into smelly molecules.[2] Wikipedia's article on body odor lists antibacterial washes among treatments, alongside deodorants and antiperspirants.[2] For acne, benzoyl peroxide is thought to kill Cutibacterium acnes through oxidative damage, loosen clogged follicles and perhaps reduce sebum.[1] No studies of benzoyl peroxide for underarm odor were found.
infobox: OTC and Rx; WHO essential medicines list

paras: The medication is mainly used for acne, alone or combined with antibiotics such as clindamycin or with retinoids such as adapalene, as a gel, cream or liquid typically at 2.5 to 10 percent.[1] Wikipedia notes higher strengths do not clearly work better than lower ones.[1] Non-medical uses include bleaching and starting polymerization in plastics and dental resins.[1]

Proponents say that because the compound kills skin bacteria, it also reduces the bacteria that turn apocrine sweat into odor. Wikipedia's body odor article describes that bacterial mechanism and lists antibacterial washes among treatments, but does not mention benzoyl peroxide.[2]

Skin irritation including redness, burning and dryness is common and increases with higher strengths, and tolerance usually builds over a few weeks.[1] About 1 in 500 people have a hypersensitivity reaction, and roughly a third of users experience phototoxicity under UVB light.[1] Contact with fabric or hair can cause permanent bleaching, including indirect contact such as via a towel.[1] Underarm skin is thin and covered by clothing, which makes bleaching of garments relevant for this use.
Brodie first prepared the compound in 1858; skin uses were reported from around 1905, uses for acne-related conditions expanded in the 1930s, and the US approved it for acne in 1960.[1]
No studies found for body odor.

timeline.event: Benjamin Collins Brodie first prepares benzoyl peroxide.[1]
